founding.title: The Landing
paragraphs: A war no one wanted, waged for reasons long since forgotten, unmade the land our grandparents called home. Those who escaped scattered — most to the southern mainland, where another people, kin in shape but not in tongue, made room for them in cities already too full.

Others looked north. Past the grey straits, to a small island the old charts named Cambrera (cam-BREH-rah). The soil is what it is, and the winters bite. But the land is unclaimed, and quiet, and what we raise here will be ours — raised by our hands, for the first time.

This is a world of iron axes and ploughshares, of timber halls and stone keeps. The great empires that built the roads are dust, and the old magics with them — shrines stand silent, and the songs of the elder days grow shorter every generation. What remains is earth, timber, and the patience to work both.
You arrive with five souls, two children, and the ship that brought you. Break ground. Keep them fed. Build something worth staying for.

klon_falls.title: The Siege of Destum
klon_falls._note: Fires when the first scripted Exarum wave lands (~year 5). The id predates the copy — it names the fall of Klon's empire, which the siege of Destum begins; Klon himself does not die until the second wave.
paragraphs: They come in on the morning tide, in a boat that should not have survived the crossing. Six of them, and one who does not wake again after they are carried up the shingle. Nobody asks where they set out from. Everyone already knows.

What they carry is worse than hunger. Destum is besieged — Destum, the old capital, whose walls the songs called unbreakable and whose gates the tax collectors of three generations rode out from. The draconian host does not raid and withdraw. It arrives, it settles, and it does not leave. Town by town, the south of Exarum has gone quiet.

Emperor Klon holds the walls himself, they say. He rides the parapet at dawn where the men can see him, and the banner still flies, and no one on that wall believes any of it will be enough. The travellers were not sent here. They simply ran until there was no more running to be done, and the sea was in front of them, and someone remembered an island on an old chart.
That evening the settlement stands at the water's edge longer than the work allows, looking south at nothing. The strait is grey and wide and it has never felt narrow before.

long_house_built.title: The Long House
paragraphs: It takes the whole summer. The ridgepole alone occupies eleven people for a day and a half, and when it finally seats, someone laughs — a high, undignified, exhausted sound — and then everyone is laughing, standing in the sawdust with their hands ruined.

The roof goes on before the first frost. Inside, the dark smells of cut pine and wet thatch, and the fire in the long pit throws light far enough up the beams that you cannot see where they end. It is the largest enclosed space any of us has stood in since the crossing. Several of the children will not go in at first. Several of the adults understand exactly why.

What changes is not the shelter. We had shelter. What changes is that there is now a place where the whole settlement can be in one room and hear one another, and so there is now a thing that must be decided together rather than simply endured. Old arguments that lived in doorways and at the edges of fields come inside and are given names.
The oldest among us sits nearest the fire without being asked. That, too, is a decision — made by no one, and by everybody.

shrine_of_anata_built.title: The Green Field and the Kind Dusk
paragraphs: We have buried no one on Cambrera. Anata's people do not put their dead into the ground to be forgotten by degrees; the body goes back to the world by fire, quickly and in the open, while everyone stands close enough to feel the heat of it. Until now we have done this at the shore, in whatever weather came, with no more ceremony than a pile of driftwood and someone remembering to speak.

The shrine is not much: dressed stone, a low wall, a pit built properly this time so the wind cannot shame us. There is no idol. Anata is the green field and the kind dusk — the goddess of the thing growing and the thing ending, which the old priests insisted were the same thing viewed from two ends. Carving her face would be a category error, and the elders would not permit it.

An elder is named keeper of the names. This is the whole of the office: she must be able to say, aloud and without notes, who has died here and who they were the child of, and she must teach it to someone younger before her own turn comes. Nothing is written down. Anata's faith has never trusted a thing that can be lost in a fire or read by a stranger.
Whether the goddess attends is not a question the settlement asks out loud. The pyre burns better in a proper pit. The names are said. Someone tends the wall. That is what a shrine is for.
